examples.name: Shroom Zoom
examples.description: Platforming with trigger-activated bounce raycasts, player impulses, and collectible sprites that follow or orbit their owner.

highlights.title: Combine a nearby trigger with a precise contact check
highlights.description: BounceTrigger callbacks enable raycasting while the player is inside a trigger and remove that system on exit. The raycast and bounce logic check downward hits against the configured mushroom entity and apply a player impulse near its surface.
highlights.context: Read it alongside BounceZoom or BounceRegular for the scene's trigger dimensions and impulse settings.

highlights.title: Turn collected items into an animated entourage
highlights.description: Follower target helpers calculate offsets around the player and positions around an orbit. followSpritesSystem interpolates each sprite toward its target, switching to orbiting when the collection is complete and rotating sprites toward their owner.
highlights.context: The scene's collection sets, follower entities, and per-player orbit timestamps supply the state for this visual behavior.

examples.name: Goal Legends
examples.description: Multiplayer penalty shootouts with server-run matches, persistent leaderboards, phase-driven cameras, and synchronized ball animations.

highlights.title: Switch cameras with match phases
highlights.description: `initGameplayCamera` selects gameplay, winner, or standard cameras from the client match snapshot. The winner camera orbits a pivot, while spectators can choose a free camera during play.
highlights.context: Follow this alongside `clientSnapshot`, the `GameState` enum, and the named scene camera pivot.

highlights.title: Coordinate a prop animation with the game state
highlights.description: `tickAnimationManager` starts a ball clip when the phase changes, chooses goal/save animations from the shot direction, and briefly hides the prop while changing clips. This path is specific to the bot kicker; human kickers carry the ball in their emotes.
highlights.context: It depends on the scene's ball model and named animation clips.

examples.name: Monster Recon
examples.description: Memory matching followed by trigger-based monster chases, with collectible progression, leaderboards, and custom bitmap text.

highlights.title: Build a chase from scene markers and trigger areas
highlights.description: `spawnHop` combines a bobbing tween, spherical trigger, sound, and billboard sprite at a selected marker. The catch handler checks that the entering entity is the local player before cleaning up and calling the reward callback.
highlights.context: Read this with the marker names, sprite atlas, and callbacks supplied to `startPrizeChase`.

highlights.title: Render custom bitmap text in ReactEcs
highlights.description: `BitmapTextLine` lays out individual glyph images using atlas UVs, glyph offsets, and kerning. The preceding measurement and wrapping helpers break text into lines by measured width.
highlights.context: The renderer needs matching bitmap-font metrics and texture assets.

examples.name: Prime Drive
examples.description: Three-lane racing with recycled scenery, distance-based record ghosts, and persistent leaderboard data.

highlights.title: Create a long race with recycled scenery
highlights.description: `setWorldOffset` and `scrollTrack` move a shared world root sideways for lane changes and wrap road decorations back ahead after they pass the player. The bike stays in place while the scenery supplies the sense of movement.
highlights.context: Read the ring builders and shared `TRACK`/`SPAWN` settings to understand spacing and wrap distances.

highlights.title: Show record ghosts relative to the player
highlights.description: `updateGhosts` places ghost bikes from their distance gap, hides ghosts outside the viewing range, and smoothly moves them into lanes away from the player.
highlights.context: This module consumes `GhostRunView` data; it displays supplied progress and does not itself record a replay.

examples.name: The Fortune Teller
examples.description: Social fortune-telling with explicit conversation-state transitions and a pivot-based cinematic camera rig.

highlights.title: Represent a reading as explicit state transitions
highlights.description: The fortune state machine lists allowed steps from category and deck selection through the reveal. `tryTransition` checks the next step, updates the session, and notifies state-entry listeners.
highlights.context: Read it with the session types and action handlers to see how a multi-step interaction is organized.

highlights.title: Build a camera rig around a scene object
highlights.description: `ensureHostPivotRig` and `startHostCinematicCamera` parent a virtual camera to a pivot under the table, choose starting and ending angles from the player's side, and activate the camera.
highlights.context: The rig depends on the table entity, configuration values, and update system in this module; those pieces explain how to frame an interaction in its scene context.

examples.name: Clean The Club
examples.description: Cooperative nightclub cleanup with shared component polling and avatar-attached props that reflect carried items.

highlights.title: Share one component scan across several systems
highlights.description: onClutterPoll gathers ClutterSync entries once per polling interval, builds an item-ID lookup, and passes the same snapshot to subscribers. Each consumer can do its own filtering and change detection.
highlights.context: This is useful for studying how to avoid repeated ECS scans; it depends on the shared schema and phase-gate polling interval, and subscriptions belong in client initialization.

highlights.title: Show another player's carried equipment
highlights.description: updateRemoteCarry attaches a prop hierarchy to the other avatar's left hand, selects a model from the current gear or hauling state, and scales the bag by its fill fraction. It also removes the hierarchy when there is nothing to display.
highlights.context: Read this with the carry message handlers, theme model lookup, and model-fit offsets: those provide the state and asset-specific positioning.

examples.name: Astro Crew
examples.description: Cooperative spaceship combat with server-owned game state, persistent progression, turret cameras, and screen-edge objective markers.

highlights.title: Point players toward off-screen objectives
highlights.description: edgePositionForBreach projects a breach direction onto the camera's horizontal axes, finds an edge of a rectangle, and clamps the icon inside the screen using the canvas aspect ratio. BreachIcon connects that position to a pulsing ReactEcs marker.
highlights.context: Read it with the scene's breach positions, active-breach state, and UI constants.

highlights.title: Add camera shake that returns to the original pose
highlights.description: shakeEntity records a base transform and combines overlapping shakes using intensity and remaining duration. CameraShakeSystem applies diminishing position and rotation offsets, then restores the base pose and removes the component.
highlights.context: The effect uses the project's amplitude constants and must be registered as an ECS system.

examples.name: Cozy Farm
examples.description: A social farming game with timed crop-growth stages, fertilizer modifiers, and repeated farms built from one entity hierarchy.

highlights.title: Turn elapsed time into crop growth stages
highlights.description: `growthSystem` derives progress from a planting timestamp, adjusts the duration for tutorial crops and fertilizer, and swaps models only when a stage changes.
highlights.context: Follow it alongside `PlotState`, `CROP_DATA`, and the model helpers in `game/actions` to see how simulation state drives visual feedback.

highlights.title: Build multiple farms from one entity hierarchy
highlights.description: `cloneEntityTree` recursively recreates a template's children, preserves local transforms, copies selected rendering components, and records each clone by name. This shows how repeated areas can share an authored layout.
highlights.context: The helper expects the scene's child map and copies an explicit component list, so new component types need deliberate handling.

examples.name: Dead Surge
examples.description: Zombie survival with weapon progression, pooled reward text, and local enemy steering around other zombies and obstacles.

highlights.title: Reuse entities for floating reward text
highlights.description: `spawnZcRewardTextAtPosition` and its pool initializer cycle through a fixed set of text entities. The `rewardTextSystem` makes them rise, face the camera, and fade before hiding them for reuse.
highlights.context: Read the scene's `RewardTextComponent` and game-time updates with these functions to understand their lifetime tracking.

highlights.title: Steer enemies around each other and simple obstacles
highlights.description: `getZombieSeparationDirection` combines repulsion from nearby zombies. `resolveZombieMovePosition` tries the desired direction, a fallback, and individual movement axes against circular brick obstacles.
highlights.context: This illustrates local steering; the behavior depends on the scene's movement entries, obstacle positions, and radius constants.

examples.name: Kick Off
examples.description: A World Cup prediction scene with charged ball kicks, immediate local motion feedback, and responsive schedule panels.

highlights.title: Connect a charged kick to immediate visual feedback
highlights.description: The charge-and-release loop combines keyboard and mobile input, grows and recolors a charge bar, sends a kick message, and starts local ball motion. `releaseOptimistic` initializes that motion.
highlights.context: Study it with the project's `prodeNet` room and ball message handlers to understand the relationship between input, feedback, and multiplayer messages.

highlights.title: Scale UI from a reference canvas
highlights.description: `layoutScale` reads `UiCanvasInformation`, compares both dimensions with a 1920×1080 design space, clamps the result, and applies an additional mobile factor.
highlights.context: It is a compact example of a shared layout helper; the limits and mobile factor are tuned for this project's panels.

examples.name: My Dear Pet
examples.description: Pet collecting with acceleration and braking for movement, plus phase-offset animation of editor-placed eggs.

highlights.title: Give moving pets acceleration and braking
highlights.description: `petMotionStep` keeps a speed per entity, limits the target speed using the remaining stopping distance, and returns a frame-sized movement step. The caller still supplies the route and updates the transform.
highlights.context: Read the arrival-distance, acceleration, and braking values in `shared/config` alongside this helper when studying its movement feel.

highlights.title: Animate editor-placed props with different phases
highlights.description: `setupEggShake` finds named egg entities, remembers their original rotations, and applies a small sine-wave rotation with a different phase for each egg. This adds variation while retaining each prop's authored orientation.
highlights.context: It depends on the egg names generated from the Creator Hub scene.

examples.name: Tower of Madness
examples.description: Timed platforming through changing tower sections, with asset preloading and a skippable camera tour of the level.

highlights.title: Preload the pieces of a changing level
highlights.description: `setupChunkPreload` deduplicates the chunk asset paths and creates temporary GLTF entities. A system watches their loading states, removes entities after loading completes or fails, and unregisters itself when none remain.
highlights.context: This illustrates managing a preload lifecycle; the asset list comes from `shared/chunks` and is specific to the tower.

highlights.title: Build a skippable camera tour around changing geometry
highlights.description: `playCinematic` adjusts camera keyframes around the current start and end chunks, then selects a virtual camera. The update system interpolates position and look-at targets and supports holding a button to skip.
highlights.context: Follow the chunk lookup helpers and `skipCinematic` to see how the tour finds its anchors and returns control to the player camera.

examples.name: Clap-to-claim dispenser
examples.description: A wearable dispenser that players claim by doing the clap emote in a trigger area.

highlights.title: Arm a dispenser while the player stands in front of it
highlights.description: Each dispenser stores its campaign in a `DispenserComponent`. A sphere `TriggerArea` in front of it sets `isActive` and shows a "clap to claim" toast on enter, and clears both on exit.
highlights.context: The campaign ID and dispenser key come from `ClaimConfig` in `src/modules/claiming/claimConfig.ts`.

highlights.title: Claim when the player plays the clap emote
highlights.description: `initClapToClaim` watches `AvatarEmoteCommand` on the player entity. When the emote is `clap`, it waits for the animation and claims from every dispenser that is currently active.
highlights.context: The claim request and response handling follow the same Rewards flow as the reward claim dispenser example.

examples.name: Data from a spreadsheet
examples.description: Scene content driven by a Google Sheet, updated without redeploying.

highlights.title: Read a published Google Sheet as JSON
highlights.description: `getSpreadsheetData` requests the sheet through the Google Visualization endpoint (`gviz/tq?tqx=out:json`), strips the `setResponse(...)` wrapper, and turns each row into an object keyed by the column headers.
highlights.context: The sheet must be shared so anyone with the link can view it. `gid` selects the tab and `headers=1` treats the first row as column names.

highlights.title: Apply a row to the scene
highlights.description: `updateFromSpreadsheet` reads one row and updates a banner `TextShape`, replaces the screen's `VideoPlayer` source, swaps the wearable shown on the dispenser, and points the dispenser's click action at the row's purchase link.
highlights.context: Column names such as `NowPlaying`, `VideoURL`, `WearableURN`, and `BuyURL` must match the sheet headers. Entities are looked up by the names given in the Creator Hub scene.

highlights.title: Cycle through rows from a Creator Hub button
highlights.description: `main` listens for the `Next` and `Previous` actions on the `Switch Artist` entity and wraps the row index around the downloaded data.
highlights.context: Uses `getActionEvents` from `@dcl/asset-packs`, so the actions are configured on the entity in the Creator Hub.

examples.name: Reward claim dispenser
examples.description: Wearable dispensers and airdrop crates that claim rewards from a Rewards campaign.

highlights.title: Request a reward with a signed fetch
highlights.description: `claimToken` throttles repeated clicks, skips dispensers already claimed successfully in this session, and checks that the player has a wallet. `requestToken` then posts the dispenser key, the current catalyst, and the player's address to the Rewards server using `signedFetch`.
highlights.context: Testing is on by default (`CONFIG_CLAIM_TESTING_ENABLED` in `src/config.ts`), which uses a bundled test campaign. To use your own, replace the placeholder campaign ID and dispenser key in `ClaimConfig` and turn testing off. See the Rewards getting-started guide for creating a campaign and dispenser.

highlights.title: Map Rewards responses to player feedback
highlights.description: `processResponse` shows a different dispenser UI for unavailable campaigns, out-of-stock dispensers, rewards already assigned, and successful claims. Uninitiated, disabled, and finished campaigns share one branch, which shows a not-started or ended screen only when the campaign config sets `startDate` or `endDate`, and a generic finished screen otherwise.
highlights.context: The UI states are defined in `dispenserUi.tsx`. Campaign start and end dates are optional fields on the campaign config.

highlights.title: Retry a claim with a captcha
highlights.description: When the Rewards server asks for a captcha, `getCaptcha` fetches a captcha image and shows it in the dispenser UI. Submitting the answer calls `claimToken` again with the captcha ID and value.
highlights.context: Whether a captcha is required is a setting of the dispenser in the Rewards dashboard.

highlights.title: Claim from an airdropped crate
highlights.description: `randomCrateSpawn` drops a crate with a parachute at a random point in the stage area. `DropCrate` raycasts down to find the ground and tweens the crate onto it, and clicking the crate claims the reward and makes it vanish.
highlights.context: The crate drop is triggered by the `Activate` action of a Creator Hub lever in `main`.

examples.name: NPC Toolkit
examples.description: Reusable NPC behaviours and dialogue UI for SDK7 scenes.

highlights.title: Separate revealing dialogue from advancing it
highlights.description: `handleDialogClick`, `rushText`, and `confirmText` first reveal the remaining characters if text is still typing. Subsequent input advances the script or selects a numeric dialogue branch, with callbacks for game actions.
highlights.context: Read this alongside the toolkit's `Dialog` data and `npcDialogComponent` state to understand how UI input drives a conversation.

highlights.title: Connect proximity and pointer input to an NPC interaction
highlights.description: `addClickReactions` and `addTriggerArea` configure pointer callbacks and a child sphere trigger, with settings for click-only activation and continuing dialogue when the player walks away. `activate` and `endInteraction` coordinate the active NPC, cooldown, dialogue, and optional player-facing behavior.
highlights.context: These functions rely on the toolkit's callback maps and tracking system.

examples.name: Flag Tag
examples.description: Multiplayer keep-away with timed rounds, persistent leaderboards, pooled projectiles, and a proximity-based lighting budget.

highlights.title: Reuse projectile visuals by model variant
highlights.description: The projectile pool pre-creates ten hidden entities for each boomerang color. Acquire and release helpers find an available entity and return it to its hidden position after stopping its sound.
highlights.context: The flight code must position acquired entities and return them when finished; the pool relies on the project's boomerang assets and sound helper.

highlights.title: Limit active lights around the player
highlights.description: proximityLightSystem checks periodically, selects the nearest lights with squared-distance comparisons and reusable arrays, and changes only lights whose active state differs. The scene caps the active set at eight and gates it through its day/night helper.
highlights.context: Read the setup and constants in the same file to understand the world-position conversion and device-specific intensity settings.

examples.name: Pigeon Deluxe
examples.description: Timed parcel delivery with pickup and drop-off areas, an avatar-mounted direction pointer, and scoring separated from delivery animation.

highlights.title: Point toward an objective while attached to an avatar
highlights.description: `initParcelDirectionPointer` and its update system attach an arrow above the avatar's name tag, calculate the world-space direction to the active target, and convert that rotation into the parent's local space. Rotation advances using `dt`, so the arrow turns toward the objective over time.
highlights.context: The target comes from the parcel system and the arrow uses the scene's `FaceDirection1.glb` asset.

highlights.title: Separate scoring from delivery animation
highlights.description: `startNewRound` and `handleSpawnAreaEnter` assign pickup and delivery roles to pads, track whether a parcel is being carried, and award points and time as soon as the delivery pad is entered. The next round starts when the drop animation finishes.
highlights.context: Read this with the scene's game timer and parcel-attachment helpers to see how gameplay state and visual feedback fit together.

examples.name: Alien Scrapyard
examples.description: Cooperative building rounds with data-defined construction puzzles and phase-driven cinematic cameras.

highlights.title: Represent build puzzles as data
highlights.description: Slot definitions describe the required part, position, scale, and label for each piece. Template helpers recenter and scale the layouts, expose a sequence of puzzles, and look up individual slots. This is useful for studying how to add new constructions through data.
highlights.context: Read it alongside the shared scene-center and part-type constants.

highlights.title: Tie a cinematic camera to round state
highlights.description: The cinematic system activates shots for countdown and performance phases, handles players joining mid-round, and releases the camera when the snapshot is stale. The final update adds round-change and elapsed-time exits before moving the camera along its shot.
highlights.context: The example depends on the client snapshot, shared timing constants, and HUD visibility helpers.

examples.name: Fastlane Bowling
examples.description: Multiplayer bowling with server-simulated physics, persistent progression, batched state updates, and mobile-scaled particle effects.

highlights.title: Batch synchronized state changes into client events
highlights.description: In `LaneWatcher.onLaneChanged`, a set collects changed lanes and schedules one flush. `flush` reads each lane's snapshot and emits state and phase-transition events. Follow this flow to understand how the scene connects synchronized components to client reactions.
highlights.context: Read it alongside the project's `LaneStore` and event-bus definitions.

highlights.title: Scale particle effects for mobile
highlights.description: `getParticleRatio` and `scaleConfig` adjust emission rates, particle limits, and burst counts using a mobile ratio while preserving the original configuration. `spawn` applies that configuration to a new emitter, with optional parenting and timed cleanup.
highlights.context: This is useful when studying how one effect configuration can serve different devices.

examples.name: Sky Chaser
examples.description: Multiplayer package-catching rounds with persistent leaderboards, pooled projectiles, and pickup placement seeded from round state.

highlights.title: Reuse projectile entities during play
highlights.description: `fireProjectile` and `getIdleProjectile` reuse inactive projectiles, create new ones when the pool is exhausted, and update only active projectiles.
highlights.context: Follow the project's `Projectile` class and event handlers for movement, collision responses, and round-end cleanup.

highlights.title: Seed pickup placement from round state
highlights.description: `onGameStart` and `getRandomPosition` use the round start time to initialize the project's random generator, then sample pickup distances and heights.
highlights.context: Read the pickup configuration and component store alongside it: mobile limits and later pickup activity affect the sequence of random calls, so a shared seed alone does not guarantee identical layouts on every client.

examples.name: Slay the Steps
examples.description: A multiplayer Festive Trail scene with custom avatars, Marketplace integration, a raycast-driven color wheel, and tracking cameras.

highlights.title: Turn a 3D pointer hit into a color selection
highlights.description: `GetLocalMousePosition` raycasts from the camera and converts the hit into the wheel's local position. `SampleColorWheel` maps its angle and radius to hue and saturation, invokes a callback, and tints the value slider.
highlights.context: The implementation uses the project's wheel meshes, HSV conversion helper, and material-node names.

highlights.title: Track a moving target with a virtual camera
highlights.description: The camera position system and tween chain periodically calculate a position relative to the player and target, then tween toward it. `TrackEntity` creates the camera with `lookAtEntity` and makes it active.
highlights.context: Read `ResetCamera` and the game's event binding for the end of the tracking lifecycle.

references.label: camera position system and tween chain

examples.name: Bloom Garden
examples.description: A cooperative garden with persistent plant state, server-clock offset estimation, and pooled petal animations.

highlights.title: Estimate the offset between server and client clocks
highlights.description: The clock helper keeps five offset samples, rejects large deviations, and converts server timestamps into local time. The watering client feeds it timestamps received through the scene's message definitions.
highlights.context: This illustrates a lightweight timing estimate; network transit time is included in the samples.

highlights.title: Let temporary effects finish naturally
highlights.description: The petal setup and controls create a reusable pool from the scene's named Petal model, then start or settle the effect. The update phases scale petals in, let them fall and rest, and shrink them before recycling. Study this when an effect should stop spawning while existing objects complete their animation.
highlights.context: Placement depends on BLOOM_CENTER and the module's timing constants.

examples.name: Slide Penguin
examples.description: Penguin sliding with timed sweeping that modifies deceleration and scoring based on distance from the target.

highlights.title: Turn sweeping into a temporary movement modifier
highlights.description: `handleSwipe` applies a cooldown to the deceleration reduction and records when that effect expires. `penguinMovementSystem` restores the base deceleration after that window, updates speed, and advances the transform using frame time.
highlights.context: Follow the project's `PenguinMovement` and `SwipeBox` components and tuning constants to understand the connection between input and motion.

highlights.title: Score how close an object lands to a target
highlights.description: `calculateDistance2D` and `calculateScore` ignore height, normalize horizontal distance against a maximum distance, and map it to a rounded score capped by `MAX_SCORE`.
highlights.context: This small module is a useful starting point for understanding proximity scoring; its inputs are the final penguin position and target position.
